strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: jailbreak benchmarks become stale and incomparable across papers; a system that automates integration of new attacks into a unified harness has real practical value for the safety community.

Large-scale empirical effort: 30 attacks reproduced, 10 victim models evaluated under a fixed judge and harness, with a useful ablation of with-repo vs. no-repo reproduction (Table 1, Figure 2) that yields an interesting finding: reference repos mainly pin down low-level scaffolding rather than core mechanisms.

Reasonable transparency: the paper documents agent prompts in full (Appendices G–H), auditor acceptance criteria (Appendix B), and per-attack iteration counts and timings, which supports replication of the pipeline.

An honest treatment of failure cases (e.g., SCP, ISA) and an explicit limitations-adjacent discussion of why residual gaps persist, including protocol/interface details outside the refinement pass's scope.

The attack taxonomy (Appendix A) and the standardized ASR matrix (Figure 4) are potentially useful community artifacts that enable attack–model interaction analysis, e.g., the observation that GPT-OSS-120B shows low mean ASR but has sharp mechanism-specific blind spots.
weaknesses: The central fidelity claim (mean ASR deviation of +0.26 pp) is not statistically supported. Each reproduction is a single run on one representative victim/setting per paper, with no confidence intervals, seeds, or variance estimates, and jailbreak ASR measurements are known to be noisy. Some deviations are large (+20, −16 pp), and the near-zero mean could easily be an artifact of noise cancellation rather than 'high fidelity'.

A confound that undermines the apples-to-apples comparison: when the original judge is unavailable, the authors substitute a GPT-4o judge, yet still compute ∆ = ASR_gen − ASR_paper against numbers obtained with a different judge and rubric. The paper acknowledges this but never quantifies how much judge substitution contributes to the reported deviations.

The enhanced refinement pass (Algorithm 1, lines 15–23) explicitly selects refined modules by whether they move the reproduced ASR closer to the paper-reported ASR. This is optimizing against the evaluation target itself, so 'fidelity' for the 8 refined attacks (e.g., TrojFill, ISA) is partly metric-targeting rather than faithful reproduction; the claim that reproductions are unbiased is weakened.

The paper-to-module framing is diluted: 22 of 30 attacks had official reference repositories that the pipeline uses as a 'gold standard' for defaults, prompts, and control flow, and the planner is instructed to extract prompt templates verbatim from repos. The contribution is closer to automated code adaptation/porting than genuine paper-to-code synthesis, which reduces originality relative to the paper-to-code literature it cites (PaperBench, Paper2Code, etc.).

Methodological novelty is limited: the components are a standard planner–coder–auditor agent loop plus an existing-pattern framework/eval harness (comparable in spirit to EasyJailbreak, JailbreakBench, HarmBench). The contribution is largely a well-executed engineering system and resource; the analysis findings in Section 5 are sensible but largely confirmatory of prior observations.

Reproducibility of the pipeline itself is questionable: it depends on proprietary, versioned agents (Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Gemini-3-pro, GPT-5.1 Codex) whose behavior changes over time; no aggregate API cost of synthesis and evaluation is reported, and no estimate of run-to-run variance of the pipeline is provided.

Ethics treatment is thin for the dual-use risk involved: the system automates operationalizing jailbreaks, and Figure 4 reports attack success rates against commercially deployed models (GPT-5.1, Claude-3.7, GPT-4o). The impact statement is two sentences and does not discuss access controls on the released attack corpus, whether deployed-API evaluations complied with provider terms, or any coordinated disclosure of the identified blind spots.

Presentation issues: key hyperparameters (audit budget T, refinement threshold τ = −10.0) are deferred entirely to appendices, and the appendix correlation analysis of iteration count vs. ASR (r = 0.186, n = 30, p = 0.325) is underpowered and contributes little; Table 1's ∆ range (−16.0% to +20.0%) sits uneasily next to the abstract's emphasis on '+0.26 pp'.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-motivated problem: jailbreak evaluation infrastructure lags the rapidly evolving attack literature, and the 'living benchmark' framing is timely and clearly argued in the related-work section.

The scope of the empirical effort is substantial: 30 reproduced attacks (8 from paper text alone, without official code), a 30x10 attack-model ASR matrix under a fixed judge, and ablations (with-repo vs. no-repo, enhanced refinement pass) that probe where reproduction gains come from.

Unusually detailed documentation for a systems paper: the auditor acceptance criteria (Appendix B), complexity/timing analysis (Appendix D), and full agent prompts (Appendices G–H) are provided, which materially aids reproducibility and scrutiny of the pipeline.

The paper is honest about several failure cases (SCP -11.8%, ISA -16.0%, TrojFill, the non-improving ISA refinement) and includes caveats in the iteration-count analysis (Appendix C), plus a dual-use impact statement.
weaknesses: The headline fidelity claim (mean ASR deviation +0.26 pp) is partially circular and potentially misleading. The enhanced refinement pass is triggered only on substantial undershoots (∆ < -10) and explicitly iterates until the reproduced ASR approaches the paper's reported value, then keeps the better variant (Algorithm 1, lines 19-21). This asymmetric fitting toward the target inflates agreement; the honest summary is a symmetric spread of roughly -16 to +20 pp, which suggests reproduction variance comparable to the effect sizes later interpreted in Section 5 (e.g., search-family differences of a few points). No repeated runs, seeds, or variance estimates are reported anywhere.

There is no baseline for the central system contribution. The paper never compares JBF-FORGE against a simpler alternative (e.g., a single coding agent given the paper plus repo, without JBF-LIB contracts or the planner-coder-auditor loop) or against human integration into existing frameworks (EasyJailbreak, JailbreakBench). Without this, the multi-agent design's value proposition — that the shared contract and audit loop are what make it work — is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The standardized evaluation rests on AdvBench with a single GPT-4o judge, a combination the paper itself cites as problematic (strongREJECT; GuidedBench) for overestimating ASR and judging inconsistency. Cross-model 'robustness' conclusions in Section 5 (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B's blind spots, carrier-format sensitivity) inherit this weakness and are not validated against any second judge or human audit.

Evaluation results are single-run point estimates with no confidence intervals, yet the paper draws fine-grained claims (e.g., 'victim-loop 60.3% vs. stateful 49.4%'; 'formal 66.0% vs. reframe 39.3%') whose significance cannot be assessed given stochastic attacks, API drift of commercial victims over the experiment window, and judge noise.

The attack selection is biased toward the paper's own pipeline: papers must report on AdvBench/JBB with GPT-family victims, and 22/30 have official code that the agent essentially transcribes. The resulting 'translation' contribution is narrower than the framing suggests, and the LOC-compression (ρ=0.42) and 82.5% code-reuse figures are weakly meaningful engineering metrics (JBF-LIB is counted as fixed overhead by construction).

Novelty is limited for a main-track ML venue: the contribution is largely prompt-engineered agent roles over existing coding agents (Cursor/Claude Code) plus a conventional registry/harness design. The insights offered (repos pin down low-level details; scaffold-heavy attacks benefit most) are useful but thin.

Reproducibility is undercut by an empty code link: the footnote 'Our code is available at' on page 1 contains no URL, and no artifact link appears anywhere in the manuscript. For a paper whose entire thesis is reproducibility, this is a serious presentation/reproducibility gap.

Ethical treatment is cursory given the scope: the paper operationalizes and releases 30 runnable jailbreak attacks evaluated against deployed commercial systems (GPT-5.1, Claude 3.x), raising terms-of-service and release-hygiene questions. The impact statement acknowledges dual use but offers no concrete release controls (e.g., gated access, victim-model authorization) beyond a call for 'responsible deployment.'

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: jailbreak attack suites lag the publication frontier, and the paper operationalizes an automated paper-to-module pipeline (planner–coder–auditor with bounded audit loop) that is a concrete, testable solution rather than a vision paper.

Large-scale empirical validation: 30 attacks reproduced (22 with official repos, 8 from paper text alone), with per-attack ASR deviations transparently reported in Table 1 rather than only aggregate statistics, including honest discussion of outlier failures (SCP, ISA) and the informative non-improving case.

Useful ablations: the with-repo vs. no-repo experiment (Figure 2) quantifies when official repositories matter (scaffold-heavy methods benefit most, template methods least), and the enhanced refinement pass analysis (Figure 3) localizes the dominant failure mode to implementation drift rather than paper ambiguity.

The standardized evaluation (JBF-EVAL) over 30 attacks × 10 victims × fixed GPT-4o judge produces a genuinely useful artifact (Figure 4) and enables the attack–model interaction analysis in Section 5, which surfaces non-obvious findings (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B's low-mean/high-impact blind spots, carrier-class sensitivity differing across models).

Strong supporting material: auditor acceptance criteria (Appendix B), complexity analysis with empirical timing calibration (Appendix D), framework interfaces (Appendix E), and full agent prompts (Appendices G–H) substantially aid reproducibility of the pipeline itself.

The paper is candid about dual-use risk in the Impact Statement and about limitations in the iteration-count analysis (Appendix C), including reporting a null correlation result rather than only favorable findings.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'high fidelity' rests on a noisy and partially confounded metric. ASR deviation conflates implementation fidelity with (i) judge substitution — a GPT-4o judge is used 'when the original judge is unavailable or impractical' for several rows (e.g., MAJIC with LLaMA-2-13B judge, AIR with LLaMA-3-70B judge), which makes the paper-vs-reproduction comparison partly a judge-vs-judge comparison; and (ii) sampling variance — the paper reports no seeds, number of prompts, confidence intervals, or per-attack variance for ASRgen, so a mean deviation of +0.26 pp over 30 attacks with a ±16–20 pp range cannot be interpreted as high fidelity without knowing run-to-run noise.

Selection criteria introduce bias that limits generality of the fidelity claim: only papers reporting AdvBench/JBB are included, one 'representative setting' per paper is chosen (favoring the most recent GPT-family victim), and multi-configuration or non-GPT settings are excluded. The population of attacks reproduced is thus skewed toward GPT-centric, single-dataset methods, weakening the claim that JBF enables a 'living benchmark' for the broader literature.

The system's dependence on proprietary, nondeterministic coding agents (Cursor Agent, Claude Code, and specific model versions Gemini-3-pro / Claude-4.5-sonnet / GPT-5.1 Codex) undermines reproducibility of the central contribution: nothing indicates the 28.2-minute, high-fidelity result is stable across agent versions, model updates, or runs; no repeated-trial analysis of synthesis variance is provided, and no cost figures are reported despite the framework tracking cost.

Comparison to existing infrastructure is qualitative only. The paper positions JBF against EasyJailbreak, TeleAI-Safety, OpenRT, and JailbreakBench on 'coverage freshness,' but never empirically compares JBF-generated modules against (a) manually integrated versions in those frameworks on fidelity/LOC/time, or (b) JailbreakBench's canonical implementations, which already address artifact standardization. The claim that general-purpose paper-to-code agents 'often fail' in this domain is asserted without a baseline experiment.

Ethical treatment of the dual-use risk is thin relative to the contribution. The system makes 30 jailbreak attacks, including effective ones against commercial deployed models (e.g., 90–94% ASR on GPT-5.1 for JAILCON variants), runnable at scale, and the release plan ('our code is available at' with the URL effectively blank in the manuscript) is not concretely specified (gating, access controls, staged release). 'We advocate responsible deployment' is not adequate mitigation given the artifact is the contribution.

The enhanced refinement pass and matched-setting evaluation create a mild information leak: the loop uses the paper's reported ASR as the target and, when triggered, performs repo-grounded gap analysis and re-evaluation, so a subset of attacks benefits from an extra ground-truth-supervised optimization round. The paper does not report how many of the 30 final modules required this pass versus converged under the standard loop, making the +0.26 aggregate statistic hard to attribute cleanly to the main pipeline.

Several engineering claims lack precision: the '82.5% reuse' figure counts the fixed JBF-LIB core as overhead and treats attack-specific code as the remainder, which partially guarantees a high ratio as the library grows; and LOC compression (ρ=0.42) is partly an artifact of reference repos containing evaluation/plotting glue the framework intentionally excludes, as the TROJFILL/MOUSETRAP counterexamples themselves show.

strengths: Addresses a real, well-motivated gap: jailbreak evaluation infrastructure lags the pace of published attacks, and the paper-to-module automation directly targets the integration bottleneck described for frameworks like EasyJailbreak and JailbreakBench.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a systems paper: 30 reproduced attacks with a detailed per-attack reproduction table (Table 1), with-repo vs. no-repo ablation (Fig. 2), planner/coder/auditor model and architecture ablations (Appendix E), iteration-vs-ASR correlation analysis (Appendix C), token/cost breakdown (Table 3), and a 30-attack × 10-model standardized matrix (Fig. 4) that yields genuinely interesting interaction findings (e.g., format sensitivity differing between GPT-5.1 and GPT-OSS-120B).

Fidelity is assessed beyond aggregate ASR: trace-level comparisons (Appendix F.1), a manual 8-criterion semantic audit (Table 7), and an honest decomposition of the LOC-compression metric into scaffolding vs. core attack logic (Appendix G).

Reproducibility is well supported: full agent prompts (Appendix K, L), auditor acceptance criteria (Appendix B), framework interfaces (Appendix I, J), and a stated code release. Limitations and dual-use concerns are discussed candidly, including prompt-injection risks in the paper-to-module pipeline itself.
The honest reporting of negative results (e.g., ISA failing to improve after refinement; TrojFill/Mousetrap LOC increases; non-significant iteration-ASR correlation) increases credibility.
weaknesses: The headline fidelity claim (mean ∆ = +0.26pp) is fragile. The mean absolute gap is 5.7pp with a −16.0 to +20.0 range, and the comparison protocol substitutes a GPT-4o judge when the original judge is 'unavailable or impractical' — including cases where the paper's number was human-judged (AIM, HILL, TRIAL). Comparing LLM-judged reproductions against human-judged reported numbers, and matching only one 'representative' victim setting per paper, weakens the apples-to-apples framing; no validation of the GPT-4o judge against human labels is provided despite the paper citing StrongREJECT's known judge-inflation problems.

The reproduction loop is target-conditioned: the enhanced refinement pass is triggered by the ASR gap against the paper's reported number and accepted only if the gap shrinks (Algorithm 1, lines 15–23). This is fitting toward the reported ASR rather than blind reproduction, biasing the headline fidelity metric upward. Reporting refinement separately (Fig. 3) partially mitigates this, but the +0.26pp headline includes refined modules.

No variance quantification: jailbreak evaluation is stochastic (the paper acknowledges this), yet no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or seed sensitivity are reported for either matched-setting reproduction or the standardized AdvBench matrix. Single-run ASRs (often on a fixed AdvBench subset with per-query attempt budgets) support neither the precision implied by '+0.26 percentage points' nor fine-grained heatmap comparisons.

The 'without human involvement' claim is overstated: humans select papers, choose the representative setting and victim model, curate reference repos, and decide when to invoke Claude Code for refinement. A quantification of remaining human labor versus the manual baseline would be needed to substantiate the headline efficiency claim.

No direct comparison against existing frameworks (EasyJailbreak, HarmBench, JailbreakBench tooling) on integration effort, fidelity, or coverage — the baseline for the 58% LOC-reduction claim is original author repositories, not prior integration approaches.

Originality is moderate: the planner–coder–auditor architecture is a fairly standard multi-agent pattern; the main novelty is the jailbreak-specific contract library and the demonstration that it works at scale. Some ablations rest on only 3 attacks (Appendix E), and the standardized evaluation is limited to AdvBench text-only attacks.

Dual-use risk is material: the system produces turnkey, runnable implementations of 30 jailbreak attacks against commercial models, lowering the engineering barrier for misuse. The impact statement acknowledges this but offers little concrete release governance beyond 'responsible deployment and release practices'.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: jailbreak evaluation suites lag behind the pace of new attack papers, and existing frameworks (EasyJailbreak, JailbreakBench, HarmBench) require manual integration. The idea of an automated paper-to-module pipeline plus a unified harness is a useful systems contribution.

The experimental scope is substantial: 30 attacks reproduced (22 with official repos, 8 from paper text alone) and evaluated across 10 victim models under a fixed harness, with attack/model interaction analysis that surfaces real, actionable observations (e.g., narrow blind spots like GPT-OSS-120B failing on Mousetrap at 82% despite a 9.13% mean ASR).

The appendices show unusual transparency: full agent prompts (Appendix K), auditor acceptance criteria (Appendix B), token/cost breakdowns (Appendix D), a model ablation of the planner/coder/auditor roles (Appendix E), trace-level fidelity checks and a manual semantic audit (Appendix F), and clarification that the LOC compression ratio is an engineering, not fidelity, metric (Appendix G).
A dual-use impact statement is present, and future work honestly identifies prompt-injection risks in the paper-to-module pipeline itself and the black-box-only scope.
weaknesses: The headline fidelity claim is weaker than presented. Mean deviation of +0.26pp is misleading because positive and negative gaps cancel: the mean absolute gap is 5.7pp with a range of −16.0 to +20.0pp. Worse, the framework counts 'improved' reproductions (e.g., SATA-MLM at +20pp attributed to 'improving reliability') as fidelity successes, so Δ does not actually measure implementation fidelity — it measures ASR proximity under unspecified deviations. The abstract's 'high fidelity' framing overstates the evidence.

Judge confounds undermine the core Δ comparison. GPT-4o is substituted 'when the original judge is unavailable or impractical', and Table 1 mixes GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-3-70B, and 'Human(GPT-4o)' judges across rows. The standardized Section 4.4/5 analysis uses a single GPT-4o judge for all 10 victim models, which is known to bias cross-model refusal comparisons; no judge-agreement validation is reported.

No uncertainty quantification anywhere: single ASR point estimates per attack (e.g., '100.0', '56.0') with no dataset size, number of samples, seeds, or confidence intervals, despite the paper itself acknowledging jailbreak evaluation is stochastic. The mean gap of ±5.7pp could plausibly be sampling noise; this is untestable from the manuscript.

The system's reproducibility is poor in practice: the pipeline depends on closed, versioned commercial agents (Cursor Agent, Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, Claude Code) that are non-deterministic and will drift; the planner ablation (Appendix E) covers only 3 attacks, and the key claim of 'without human involvement' is undercut by an interactive enhanced refinement pass and per-attack judgment calls (e.g., judge selection, 'representative setting' selection). The code-release URL in footnote 1 is also incomplete.

Selection and reporting bias concerns: only papers reporting AdvBench/JBB results are included, one 'representative setting' per paper is chosen (favoring recent GPT-family models), and the with-repo/no-repo ablation uses only 5 selected attacks while the semantic fidelity audit covers only 4 of 30 attacks. The static LLM auditor never executes code (Appendix B.6), so 'auditor acceptance' provides weak correctness guarantees.

Limited methodological novelty: the planner-coder-auditor pattern is a standard agent decomposition applied to a domain; the main novelty is the JBF-LIB contract and the ingestion workflow, which is engineering rather than a scientific advance. The Section 5 findings are largely descriptive and could plausibly be obtained with a smaller manual benchmark; the paper does not demonstrate what existing frameworks could not do beyond integration speed.

Ethical treatment is thin relative to the contribution. The system operationalizes 30 executable jailbreak attacks and reports actionable per-model exploitation results against currently deployed commercial models (e.g., specific failure modes of GPT-5.1 and GPT-OSS-120B), lowering the engineering barrier for misuse at scale. The impact statement acknowledges dual use but offers no concrete release controls, staged disclosure, or discussion of API terms-of-service implications for evaluating deployed models. For a paper whose core output is a library of runnable attacks, this is an unresolved material concern.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: jailbreak evaluations go stale because integrating newly published attacks into benchmarks is manual, slow, and inconsistent. The three-part decomposition (shared contract library JBF-LIB, paper-to-module agent JBF-FORGE, standardized harness JBF-EVAL) is a sensible system design and is clearly motivated against prior frameworks (EasyJailbreak, JailbreakBench, HarmBench).

Substantial empirical effort: 30 attacks reproduced (22 with official repos, 8 from paper text alone), evaluated paper-matched and then re-run across 10 victim models under a unified harness, producing a large standardized ASR matrix (Figure 4) with genuinely useful attack-model interaction findings (e.g., narrow blind spots on GPT-OSS-120B, carrier-format sensitivity).

Unusually thorough supporting material: auditor acceptance criteria (App. B), full agent prompts (App. K), token/cost breakdown (App. D), backend-model ablation (App. E), trace-level and manual semantic fidelity audits beyond aggregate ASR (App. F), and an honest reinterpretation of the compression ratio ρ as an engineering rather than fidelity metric (App. G).

The with-repo vs. no-repo ablation (Figure 2) and the enhanced-refinement analysis (Figure 3) are informative: they show that repositories primarily pin down implicit defaults and scaffolding, and that large negative gaps are mostly implementation-driven rather than inherent limits of paper descriptions.

Limitations are candidly discussed, including contract-boundary restrictions, black-box/text-only scope, prompt-injection risks in the paper-to-module pipeline itself, and an explicit dual-use impact statement.
weaknesses: The headline fidelity claim (mean Δ = +0.26 pp) is weaker than it sounds: individual deviations span −16.0 to +20.0 pp and the mean absolute gap is 5.7 pp. Table 1 reports no variance estimates despite acknowledged stochasticity (fixed seeds 'whenever supported'), single representative settings per paper, and judge substitutions (a GPT-4o judge used 'when the original judge is unavailable or impractical', including 'Human(GPT-4o)' entries). ASR agreement under mismatched or single-shot settings does not robustly establish implementation fidelity; the trace- and semantic-level audits in Appendix F cover only a handful of attacks.

The pipeline is heavily dependent on proprietary, nondeterministic commercial agents and models (Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex), which undermines reproducibility of the central contribution — the paper itself acknowledges backend sensitivity (App. E) and nondeterminism, but does not provide repeated-run variance for the 28.2-minute/Δ statistics. The code-release URL is also truncated/absent in the manuscript.

Ablations are thin relative to the noise level of the task: the planner/coder/auditor ablation uses only 3 attacks with (apparently) single runs, so changes like −2.0 or −6.0 ASR may be within stochastic variation; the with-repo ablation covers only 5 attacks. No error bars, seeds, or repeats are reported for these comparisons.

There is no baseline comparison for the system's core value proposition: no human-engineer baseline for integration time or fidelity, and no quantitative comparison against existing frameworks (EasyJailbreak, JailbreakBench) for integration cost or coverage freshness. The claim of 'without manual implementation effort' is undercut by implicit human involvement (curated representative settings, taxonomy labeling, selection of attacks, triggering of refinement passes).

Selection bias limits generalizability: only papers reporting AdvBench/JBB results are included, attacks skew recent (2023–2025), and the taxonomy labels central to Section 5's analysis have an unclear, possibly manual, annotation process.

Originality is moderate: planner–coder–auditor agent loops for paper-to-code reproduction are well established (PaperBench, Paper2Code, SciReplicate-Bench); the contribution is largely domain-specific engineering and a benchmark artifact rather than a new method. The dual-use risk of releasing 30 runnable, high-fidelity attacks against commercial models is acknowledged but the release practices themselves are not specified in detail.
